name: Hassan Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm the office administrator at Brookfield Construction, a builder with about 80 staff doing schools, warehouses and the odd housing block. I'm in the head office on the industrial estate by 7:30, because the site foremen ring early about deliveries. Most of my morning is the schedule: which crew is on which site, which skip lorry comes when, and who's booked on which safety course.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And the rest of the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paperwork and chasing. Subcontractor insurance certificates, timesheets, purchase orders, the planning office's forms, and the inspection bookings. About a year ago I set up an AI assistant that reads the delivery emails and drafts the next day's schedule, so I spend my time checking it instead of typing it. Linda Okafor, the operations director, calls it 'Hassan's robot', even though it's just software.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy fixing things that waste people's time; that's my favourite part. What wears me out is foremen who still send photos of handwritten timesheets at ten at night. On Saturdays I also do the books for my dad's bakery on Mill Street, so my week is pretty full, but I like it full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, because for me AI isn't hype; I use it every day. But I can picture a world where it stays at the level of my little scheduling helper. My boss Linda calls my scheduling helper 'Hassan's robot', even though it's just software I set up myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a good tool, use it, but don't expect it to build the warehouse for you. At work I'd probably show the younger lads in the office a few more tricks. Online I'd post the odd how-to, because I like that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm in a strong spot. I'm the person here who makes the tools work, I'm paid well for an admin, and I've got my flat plus about a year of pay saved. If nothing big changes, I just keep being useful and keep getting raises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push Linda to let me roll the scheduling assistant out to the purchase orders, which could save maybe a day a week. I'd keep overpaying the flat, an extra 400 a month, to clear it before I'm 40. And I'd set up the same email helper at my dad's bakery so he stops ringing suppliers by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit bored, if I'm honest, because I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned overpaying the flat. Is there any money worry in your life right now, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, touch wood. My dad helped with the deposit at 24, which I'm grateful for, and I've never been one to spend on cars or holidays. The only thing on my mind is the bakery, because my dad is 61 and his knees are going, and someone will have to decide what happens to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Pete Marsh, our longest-serving foreman, who still does everything on paper. Pete isn't at risk from AI, he's at risk from refusing to send his timesheets properly. I'd sit with Pete for an hour and show him the phone app, and he'd grumble and then use it.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, but it won't build the warehouse for you.
I'd keep posting **how-to tips** online and teaching the younger office staff.
think: I'm in a **strong spot**, because I'm the one who makes the tools work here.
With my flat and **a year saved**, a quiet AI world just means more raises.
do: Roll the scheduling assistant out to **purchase orders**, saving about a day a week.
Keep overpaying the flat by **400 a month** to clear it before 40.
Set up an **email helper** at my dad's bakery for supplier orders.
feel: **Calm**, and a little bored, because he enjoys it when things are moving.
S0.quote: My boss Linda calls my scheduling helper 'Hassan's robot', even though it's just software I set up myself.
fieldNote: He already sees himself as **the tools person**, so a plateau feels like a missed opportunity.
His only real worry is **his dad's bakery**, not his own job or money.
He'd help colleagues like Pete **one to one** rather than leave them behind.

steps.text: Extend the scheduling assistant to purchase orders at Brookfield
Overpay the flat by 400 a month
Keep running site schedules and inspection bookings as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels like it's already half happening, honestly. I've been doing the booking and checking part myself with AI for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the moment for people in offices to learn the tools, and that complaining won't stop it. I'd probably say it a bit bluntly, to be honest, which gets me in trouble with my mum. Online I'd share how I cut our schedule time in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office shrinks from five people to three, and I'm one of the three, because I'm the one running the systems. That's not a nice thing to know about your colleagues. Joanne in accounts payable is the one I'd worry about, because her whole job is checking invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Linda to make my role 'systems and scheduling coordinator' with a pay rise to match, and I'd do a short online course in project controls, maybe 600, to understand the cost side. I'd quietly help Joanne learn the invoice tool so she can move to supplier relationships. And I'd start charging two small builders I know for setting up their scheduling, a few hundred a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly for other people. For me it feels like a ladder, which is a strange thing to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it feels like a ladder for you. Is there any part of your own job that worries you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checking part, a bit. Right now my value is that I set it up and check it, but if the checking gets good enough, Linda might ask why she needs me full time. That's why I'd move towards the cost and planning side quickly, before anyone asks the question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help people like Joanne?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firstly Joanne herself, and her family, and then the firm, because Brookfield got the savings. I don't think the government should pay people to sit at home, but I'd back the firm paying for retraining, like an apprenticeship for older workers. My dad retrained as a baker at 35 with no help from anyone, and he's done fine.

say: I'd say office workers should **learn the tools** now, because complaining won't stop this.
Online I'd share how I **halved our schedule time** using AI.
think: I think the office shrinks **from five to three**, and I'm one of the three.
I'd worry most for **Joanne in accounts**, whose whole job is checking invoices.

Take a **project controls** course online, about 600, to learn the cost side.
Charge two **small builders** a few hundred each to set up their scheduling.
feel: **Uneasy** for colleagues, while privately seeing a **ladder** for himself.

fieldNote: He's candid that the shrinking office is a **ladder for him** and a threat to others.
He blames no one; he'd put responsibility on **the worker and family** first, then the firm.
He spots his own weak point, **the checking part**, and plans to move before it's noticed.
His father's **self-made retraining** is the model he holds up for everyone.

steps.text: Take over Brookfield's AI scheduling tools as coordinator, with a raise

Set up scheduling tools for two small builders for a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Two years. That's not a ladder anymore, that's the floor going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say the same as always, adapt or get left behind, but I'd be quieter about it, because people would be scared and it's not kind to lecture scared people. At work I'd tell the foremen their jobs are safer than mine for now. Online I'd probably stop posting how-tos, because it'd feel like dancing on graves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my office job is gone by 2028, and the systems role I built goes with it, because AGI doesn't need me to set it up. The site side is different: the foremen and labourers have until about 2031 before robots can do their work. So the place to be for those three years is on site, not in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask Linda to put me on site as an assistant site manager, even at a pay cut, and I'd start the site management course straight away. I'd stop overpaying the flat and keep that 400 a month in cash, because a year saved suddenly feels short. And I'd sit down with my dad about the bakery, because a bakery is hands-on and local, and that might be the safest thing our family owns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because I've got money and a plan, but my stomach would be tight for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take a pay cut to go on site. How much are you prepared to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fifth, for a year or two. I live cheaply, and the flat is a third paid off, so I can do that. I won't sit in an office that's being emptied and hope I'm the last one switched off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the bakery. Would you actually take it over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have to. My dad's knees won't last, and the bakery on Mill Street has customers who've come every morning for twenty years. In two years I'd rather be learning to run ovens than waiting for a computer to finish my old job. People still want bread made by a person they know, at least until 2031.

say: I'd still say adapt or **get left behind**, but more quietly to scared people.
I'd stop posting **how-to tips**, because it would feel like dancing on graves.
think: My office job and **systems role** both end by 2028, because AGI doesn't need me.
Site work has until about **2031**, so those three years should be spent on site.
do: Ask Linda for an **assistant site manager** post, even with a pay cut.
Stop overpaying the flat and keep **400 a month** in cash.
Sit down with my dad about **taking over** the bakery on Mill Street.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight stomach, but steadied by **savings** and a plan.
S2.quote: I won't sit in an office that's being emptied and hope I'm the last one switched off.
fieldNote: The two-year card flips his outlook from **ladder** to floor giving way.
He reasons clearly about the **three-year robot gap** and moves towards hands-on work.
His father's **bakery** turns from a worry into a possible lifeline for the family.
He softens his public tone, refusing to **lecture scared people**.

steps.text: Move from the office to an assistant site manager post at Brookfield

Keep the 400 flat overpayment in cash savings instead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That I can work with properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it, and a trap if you don't. At work I'd push for the firm to train the office staff now, while there's time, instead of letting people go in a panic in 2030. Online I'd go back to sharing tips, because then it actually helps people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office job still goes, just around 2031. But with five years I could get fully qualified as a site manager and have three or four years of experience before AGI arrives, and robots for site work aren't due until about 2034. That's a long runway for someone who's 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the site management course in the evenings, about 1,800, and ask Linda for a split role, half office and half on site. I'd keep overpaying the flat, because I'd want it cleared by the time things get rough. And I'd help my dad put an ordering app into the bakery now, so it's worth more if we ever sell or I take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Busy and a bit restless, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go back to sharing tips online. Isn't that a bit at odds with the job going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but no. The tools will take the office job either way; the question is whether people use the five years. I'd rather someone in an office like mine learns early than finds out on the day they're called in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about family plans? Does five years change anything there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be married with a family by about 32, God willing, and I'd want my job sorted before that. So five years pushes me to get settled on the site side first and then think about a wedding. My mum won't love waiting, but she'd understand a man getting his work in order first.

say: I'd say five years is **a gift** if you use it and a trap if you don't.
At work I'd push Brookfield to **train office staff** now, not cut them in a panic.
think: The office job still goes around **2031**, just later.
Qualifying as a **site manager** gives me years of experience before robots arrive around 2034.
do: Start an evening **site management** course this year, about 1,800.
Ask Linda for a **split role**, half office and half on site.
Put an **ordering app** into my dad's bakery to raise its value.
feel: **Uneasy**, busy and a bit restless, but not scared.
S3.quote: My mum won't love waiting, but she'd understand a man getting his work in order first.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan into a **long runway** rather than an emergency move.
His **traditional timeline** puts settled work before marriage and children.
He argues sharing tips helps others use the time, seeing **early learning** as kindness.

steps.text: Take an evening site management course costing about 1,800
Ask Linda for a half-office, half-site role
Keep overpaying the flat to clear it early
Install an online ordering app at the Mill Street bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a different man, practically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so there's no excuse, and I'd mean it for firms and families both. I'd keep sharing how-tos and maybe run a free evening session at the community centre for small business owners. People round here respect someone who teaches rather than preaches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. In ten years I could be a site manager, or running the bakery, or even running my own small firm that sets up AI for builders and trades. The office job ends by 2036, and robots on site come around 2039, but I'd have moved twice by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing at Brookfield for now, and build the side business setting up scheduling and ordering tools for small firms, aiming for ten clients in the first year. I'd keep overpaying the flat and put a bit into shares each month. And I'd still do the site management course over two or three years, as a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Excited, even. This is the version where being early actually pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. Is there anything in this version that would still keep you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only my dad, really. The bakery will need a decision in the next few years whatever happens with AI, and I'm not sure I want to spend my thirties at 4 a.m. ovens. That's a family question, not an AI one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own children to study, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade first, then whatever they like. I'd want my children to know how to make something with their hands, like my dad does, and to use the tools without being scared of them. Being able to make bread or wire a house is worth more than another degree.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for firms or families to be caught out.
I'd run a **free evening session** at the community centre for small businesses.
think: In ten years I could be a **site manager**, a baker or running my own firm.
The office job ends by 2036, but I'd have **moved twice** before robots arrive.
do: Build a **side business** setting up AI tools, aiming for ten small clients.
Keep overpaying the flat and put **a bit into shares** each month.
Take the **site management** course slowly as a safety net.
feel: **Calm**, even excited, because being early finally pays off.
S4.quote: Being able to make bread or wire a house is worth more than another degree.
fieldNote: With a decade, he sees **several paths** and treats AGI as an opportunity.
His remaining worry is **the family bakery**, which he calls a family question, not an AI one.
He'd give his children a **trade first**, echoing his father and his traditional views.

steps.text: Sign up ten small firms for paid scheduling and ordering setups
Put a set amount into shares each month
Take the site management course over two or three years
Keep running the Brookfield office schedule for now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd go under, I've got savings and the flat, but because there's no time to move properly and everyone around me would be scrambling at once. What would help is firms getting on with retraining now, and short, paid site apprenticeships for office people who want to move to hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about small family businesses like my dad's. Everyone talks about big companies and AI, but bakeries and corner shops are where a lot of us will end up. A good bakery is worth more to a street than a smart office.

headlineQuote: A good bakery is worth more to a street than a smart office.
portrait: Hassan, 27, runs scheduling and paperwork at **Brookfield Construction** and built its AI scheduling helper himself.
He owns a **flat** helped by his dad, has about a year saved and does his dad's bakery books on Saturdays.
He sees slow AI change as **a ladder** for himself, while worrying for colleagues whose jobs are checking.
Fast AGI pushes him **onto site** and towards the family bakery, using the three-year robot gap.
With ten years he's **calm and excited**, planning a side business setting up AI for small firms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because there'd be no time to move and everyone would scramble.
whatWouldHelp: Firms starting **retraining now**, before cuts arrive in a panic.
Short, paid **site apprenticeships** for office workers who want to move to hands-on work.
